sites.seoTitle: Morse Code Trainer – Learn and Practice Morse Code
about: Learn Morse code by tapping it out yourself. Press and hold the spacebar to key in Morse: a quick tap makes a dot and a longer hold makes a dash. Pause briefly between letters and a little longer between words, and the trainer decodes what you sent into text as you go.
Open the cheat sheet for the full A to Z alphabet in Morse code, and try practice mode when you are ready to test yourself.

Morse code was developed by Samuel Morse and Alfred Vail for the electric telegraph in the 1830s and 1840s. The timing follows simple rules: a dash lasts three times as long as a dot, the gap between letters is three dots long, and the gap between words is seven. The distress signal SOS (··· ––– ···) was picked because it is easy to send and hard to mistake.

sites.seoTitle: Roman Numeral Converter – Numbers to Roman Numerals and Back
about: A Roman numeral converter that works both ways. Type a regular number to see it in Roman numerals, or type Roman numerals to turn them back into a number. Every conversion comes with an itemized breakdown showing which numerals add up to the total.
It handles everything from 1 (I) to 3,999 (MMMCMXCIX), the largest number you can write in standard Roman numerals. There is no zero: the Romans never had a numeral for it.

How it works: I is 1, V is 5, X is 10, L is 50, C is 100, D is 500, and M is 1,000. A smaller numeral before a larger one is subtracted, so IV is 4 and XC is 90. Fun fact: many clock faces show 4 as IIII instead of IV, a tradition that is still common on watches and clocks today.

Some character limits worth knowing: a post on X (Twitter) is limited to 280 characters, a classic SMS text message holds 160, and Google usually shows about 150 to 160 characters of a page description in search results.

sites.seoTitle: Reaction Time Test – How Fast Are You?
about: A simple reaction time test. Click, tap, or press the spacebar to start, then wait for the screen to turn green. The moment it does, react as fast as you can. The test shows your time in milliseconds, plus your best time, your average, and how many attempts you have made.
The green light shows up after a random delay of two to six seconds, so you cannot guess the rhythm. If you click before it turns green, it counts as too soon and you start that round again.

Most people land somewhere between 200 and 300 milliseconds. Under 220 ms is very quick, and anything under 150 ms usually means you guessed. Sleep, caffeine, and practice all make a real difference, so try it a few times.

sites.seoTitle: White Noise Generator – White, Pink & Brown Noise, Rain and Fan
about: A free white noise generator and ambient sound mixer. Turn on white, pink, or brown noise, rain, thunder, or a fan hum, set the level of each one, and mix them into whatever background sound helps you focus, relax, or fall asleep.
Every sound is synthesized in your browser rather than played from a recording, and it keeps going for as long as you leave the tab open.

The difference between the noise colors: white noise has equal energy at every frequency, which makes it sound bright and hissy. Pink noise drops off as the pitch rises and sounds softer, a bit like steady rain. Brown noise drops off even faster and sounds like a deep rumble. Brown noise is named after Brownian motion, and the botanist Robert Brown, not the color.

sites.seoTitle: Perfect Circle Test – Can You Draw a Perfect Circle?
about: Draw a circle freehand around the dot and get a score out of 100, to one decimal place. The score measures how far your line drifts from a perfect circle and takes off points for a gap between where you started and where you stopped.

Use a mouse, a trackpad, or your finger. Draw the whole loop in one stroke, keep the dot inside it, and do not draw too small. Your personal best is saved in your browser so you can keep trying to beat it.

Fun fact: according to the Renaissance writer Giorgio Vasari, when the Pope asked the painter Giotto for a sample of his work, Giotto sent back a single circle drawn freehand in red paint. It was apparently so perfect that it won him the commission.

sites.seoTitle: Online Ruler – Actual Size Ruler in cm and Inches
about: An actual-size ruler on your screen, in centimeters and inches. Screens come in so many sizes and pixel densities that a ruler drawn in pixels is almost never the right size. So the first step is calibration: hold any bank or credit card against the screen and drag the knob until the outline matches the card.

Once it is calibrated, drag anywhere to measure from point to point, or drag the ruler itself to move it around. You can recalibrate at any time, or skip calibration and trust the guess if you do not need exact measurements.

Why a bank card? Almost every payment card in the world is the same size: 85.60 mm by 53.98 mm, set by the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 standard. That makes it a handy reference object that nearly everyone has in their pocket.

sites.seoTitle: Online Metronome – Free Metronome with Tap Tempo
about: A free online metronome for music practice. Set any tempo from 30 to 260 BPM with the slider or the plus and minus buttons, or tap the TAP button along with a song and the metronome will work out the tempo for you. Three taps is enough.

Choose a time signature of 2/4, 3/4, 4/4, or 6/8, and the first beat of each bar gets an accent. The current tempo marking, from largo to presto, is shown under the BPM. Keyboard shortcuts: the spacebar starts and stops the metronome, and T taps the tempo.

Fun fact: Johann Maelzel patented the metronome in 1815, and Beethoven was one of the first composers to write metronome markings into his music. That is why old sheet music sometimes says "M.M." before a tempo: it stands for Maelzel's Metronome.

sites.seoTitle: Hearing Test – How High Can You Hear?
about: A high-frequency hearing test you can take in your browser. A tone starts at 8,000 Hz and rises toward 22,000 Hz. Press the button the moment you can no longer hear it. You get three tries, and your result is the median, along with a rough estimate of your "hearing age."

Use headphones at a comfortable volume. Many laptop and phone speakers cannot play much above 16,000 Hz, so the result can say more about your speakers than your ears. This is a fun experiment, not a medical hearing test. If you are worried about your hearing, see an audiologist.

People with young, healthy ears can hear from about 20 Hz up to around 20,000 Hz. The top of that range drops gradually with age, which is why the "Mosquito" anti-loitering device, which plays a tone near 17,400 Hz, mostly bothers teenagers.

sites.description: A pocket knife for images — fold out the crop blade, the filter glass, the resize scissors. Everything happens on your device.

sites.name: Lucky Chest
sites.description: Tap the chest. Sometimes it upgrades. Paperclips, a good stick, the other sock — collect them all in your binder.

sites.name: Eye Chart
sites.description: A perfectly normal vision test — until the rows you squint at stop being letters and start being about you.

sites.name: Shortwave
sites.description: Tune a late-night radio through the static. 72 stations are hiding out there — some only broadcast after dark.

sites.name: Scratchers
sites.description: An endless supply of scratch-off tickets. The $1 ticket is always free. The rest is between you and the odds.

sites.name: Cube Loader
sites.description: An infinite boot animation. Roll the cube in any direction, forever. The console never arrives.

sites.name: Hello
sites.description: It says hello. Click and it says hello in another language — then another, and another, from all over the world.

sites.name: Etch A Sketch
sites.description: Twist the knobs to drag one unbroken line across the silver screen — then shake it clean. Diagonals are a two-handed negotiation.

sites.name: Clicker Pen
sites.description: A retractable pen that clicks perfectly, forever. The counter never forgets. The warranty is void.

sites.name: Spend the National Debt
sites.description: You've been handed the entire US national debt. Spend it on jets, islands, and aircraft carriers — the clock keeps ticking up faster than you can.

sites.name: Spend Your Life
sites.description: Your budget isn't money — it's the hours you have left. Spend them on sleep, meetings, guitar, and falling in love, and watch the clock drain.

sites.name: QR Wall
sites.description: An infinite wall of QR codes. Drag to wander, tap any one, and it takes you somewhere real.

sites.name: Wet Cement
sites.description: Leave your mark in fresh cement before it sets. Build a sidewalk of little memories.

sites.name: Under the Rug
sites.description: Lift the corner. Discover what has been swept underneath. Try not to startle the residents.

sites.name: Window Seat
sites.description: Wipe a foggy train window and watch the world roll by. There is no hurry.

sites.name: Horrible Forms
sites.description: Fill out one terribly designed form field at a time. A birthday slider. A shuffling keyboard. A checkbox that works half the time.

sites.name: The Seating Chart
sites.description: Plan the wedding reception seating chart while the family group chat adds one new demand per round. Aunt Deb will not sit with Uncle Ray.

sites.name: The Group Trip
sites.description: Plan the friend group trip — dates and destination — while the group chat adds one new demand per round. Sam is not flying.

sites.name: The Group Photo
sites.description: Arrange the family for the wedding photo while the group chat adds one new demand per round. Tall people in back. Grandma’s good side is her right.

sites.name: The Commit Message
sites.description: Write one commit message that passes every check. The linter adds a new rule after every push. Eventually it has to be a haiku.

sites.name: Pixel Peel
sites.description: There is a photo inside the circle. A pug, a tiger, a typewriter. Move your mouse over it until the circle gives up.

sites.name: Wreck This Page
sites.description: Our homepage, fully destructible. Hammer it, shoot it, bomb it. The Restore button pretends none of it happened.

sites.name: Keyboard Fireworks
sites.description: Every key is a note and a firework. Type a sentence and it becomes a small song and a light show.

sites.name: Endless Giraffe
sites.description: A giraffe. Mostly neck. Scroll down and see how far it goes.

sites.name: Terms and Conditions
sites.description: Please read and agree to the Terms and Conditions. All of them. Some of them are a test.

sites.name: Who Said It?
sites.description: A fortune cookie, a horoscope, a cat calendar, or a LinkedIn thought leader? Seven quotes a day. Guess who said it.

sites.name: Unsubscribe
sites.description: Try to unsubscribe from The Daily Spoon, a newsletter about spoons. One wrong click and you are resubscribed to everything.

sites.name: Pointing People
sites.description: Stop your cursor anywhere. Someone will point at it.

sites.name: Dominoes
sites.description: Draw a line and dominoes stand up along it. Flick the first one and watch the whole thing go.

sites.name: Turbo Ball
sites.description: Side-view car soccer. Boost, jump, flip, drive up the walls and hit an enormous ball into a goal.

sites.name: Draw a Track
sites.description: Draw a racetrack with your finger, then race it. Beat your own ghost, or take on the daily track.

sites.name: Sumo Cars
sites.description: Two cars. One ring. Push the other one out. Best of five, against the computer or a friend on the same keyboard.

sites.name: Brawlers
sites.description: A platform fighter. Sixteen fighters, three stages, three stocks each. Rack up damage, then knock them off the edge.
